stops.name: Würzburg, the country the Latin gives away
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the year is an ordering device only. No document names Adam's birthplace, his parents, or his year of birth. Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin and the Neue Deutsche Biographie both place his origin in eastern Franconia or western Thuringia, perhaps near Würzburg, arguing from name forms, his attention to the Main-country missionary saints, and verbal affinities with Main-Werra material. The sources say only 'probably before c. 1050'. An early scholium in manuscript C2, itself perhaps of 1085-1090 or later, says the author came from Germania superior, Upper Germany, and no more.
stops.campa: No register records the birth. What the man leaves instead is a Latin that keeps its own address: Sallust for the shape of a sentence, and a warmth toward Gall, Emmeram and Kilian, the saints of the Main country, that a stranger would not bother to feel. Scholars reading those habits set his cradle in eastern Franconia or western Thuringia, somewhere within a few days' ride of Würzburg. One early note in one manuscript says the author came from Upper Germany. That is the whole of the record.
sources: Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin, 'Adam Bremensis' (medieval.wiki.uib.no)
Neue Deutsche Biographie, 'Adam von Bremen' (deutsche-biographie.de/gnd11850052X.html)
Bernhard Schmeidler, MGH SS rer. Germ. 2 (dmgh.de), for the C2 scholium
suggested_refs: The cathedral quarter of Würzburg, the nearest named place in the modern reconstruction of his origin

stops.name: Bamberg, the cathedral school that may have made him
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the source that proposes it disclaims it. Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin states that whether Adam visited the then famous cathedral school of Bamberg cannot be assured. The contents of his education are inferred securely from the Gesta itself; the building he sat in is not. The 1065 correspondence between Bamberg clergy and Archbishop Adalbert is real but has never been shown to be his road north.
stops.campa: Whoever taught him taught him thoroughly: grammar and rhetoric, the Fathers, canon law, biblical exegesis, the geography of Solinus and Martianus Capella, and enough Sallust that the cadence never leaves him. Bamberg's cathedral school is the leading candidate, famous in these decades and in correspondence with Archbishop Adalbert of Hamburg-Bremen in 1065, which would be a plain enough road north for a promising clerk. The scholar who proposes it says in the same breath that it cannot be assured.
sources: Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin, 'Adam Bremensis'
Neue Deutsche Biographie, 'Adam von Bremen'
suggested_refs: Bamberg cathedral and its eleventh-century school, one of two standing conjectures for Adam's formation

stops.name: Magdeburg, the school an older tradition gave him
stops.date_confidence: tradition, and a contradiction left standing. English Wikipedia states flatly that Adam is believed to have come from Meissen and that it is probable he was taught at the Magdeburger Domschule. Modern specialist synthesis treats this Upper Saxon line as superseded by the Franconia and Thuringia hypothesis. Neither is documented. The attribution of the Meissen hypothesis to Wilhelm Wattenbach, which circulates in some summaries, could not be verified in Tschan or the NDB and is not repeated here.
stops.campa: A second tradition, nineteenth century in origin and still printed in the English encyclopedias, sends him to school here instead and gives him Meissen for a birthplace. It has never been formally retired, which is the only reason he stands here at all. Nothing in Adam's own text prefers Upper Saxony to Franconia, and nothing rules it out. Two reconstructions face each other over the same silence, each built out of the same missing document, and the choice between them gets made on the sound of his Latin.
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Adam of Bremen'
Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin, 'Adam Bremensis'
Neue Deutsche Biographie, 'Adam von Bremen'
suggested_refs: Magdeburg cathedral school, the Upper Saxon hypothesis of Adam's education

stops.name: Bremen, received in the twenty-fourth year of Adalbert
stops.date_confidence: attested by Adam himself in the prologue, and the only firmly dated event of his life before 1069. He gives the twenty-fourth pontifical year of Archbishop Adalbert, which Tschan resolves to the window between the beginning of May 1066 and the end of April 1067. The Bremen pin 53.0759, 8.8072 is the canonical one already used across the Rimbert file.
stops.campa: He comes north to a see that governs, on paper, every church between the Elbe and the pole. Archbishop Adalbert takes him into the cathedral chapter in the twenty-fourth year of his pontificate, which is to say between the beginning of May 1066 and the end of April 1067. In the prologue Adam signs himself only as A., least canon of the holy church of Bremen. He is a southerner among Saxons and says so before anyone else can: proselitus et advena, a proselyte and a stranger.
stops.quote: I, a proselyte and stranger, did not appear ungrateful for having been granted so great a favor.
stops.quote_source: Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum, prologue, tr. Francis J. Tschan
sources: Adam of Bremen, Gesta, prologue, tr. Francis J. Tschan (archive.org/details/historyofarchbis00adam_0)
Tschan, translator's introduction
Neue Deutsche Biographie, 'Adam von Bremen'
suggested_refs: St Petri Dom, Bremen, the cathedral chapter Adam entered in 1066 or 1067

stops.name: Bremen, master of the schools
stops.date_confidence: attested with a caveat the sources themselves supply. A charter of 11 June 1069 was written and signed for Adalbert by an Adam magister scolarum. Tschan says Adam was perhaps also given charge of the school, 'for an Adam magister scolarum wrote and signed a document'; the NDB records him as Domscholaster in 1069. The identification with the chronicler rests on a name, a title and a date standing together, not on any statement of authorship.
stops.campa: On the eleventh of June an archiepiscopal charter is drawn and signed by an Adam magister scolarum, Adam master of the schools. Nothing in the document says that this Adam wrote a book; the identification rests on a name, a title and a date standing together on one sheet. Most scholars take the schoolmaster and the chronicler for one man, which would put the cathedral school of Bremen and its boys in his charge within three years of his arrival, along with occasional work in the archbishop's chancery.
sources: Tschan, translator's introduction to the Gesta
Neue Deutsche Biographie, 'Adam von Bremen'
suggested_refs: The archiepiscopal charter of 11 June 1069 subscribed by Adam magister scolarum

stops.name: Bremen, Rimbert's books on the desk
stops.date_confidence: attested as source-dependence, undated as an event. Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin identifies the anonymous Vita Rimberti and Rimbert's own Vita Anskarii as Adam's material for Gesta I.34-44. Rimbert's lost letter to Ratramnus of Corbie, sent before 865, is attested through Ratramnus's surviving reply. There is no surviving evidence that Adam had that reply in front of him when he wrote the cynocephali passage of Book IV, and this file does not claim he did.
stops.campa: For the ninth century he has two lives to work from: the Vita Anskarii, written by Rimbert, who succeeded Ansgar in this see, and the anonymous Vita Rimberti written for Rimbert in turn. Out of them he builds chapters thirty-four to forty-four of his first book. Rimbert had once sent a letter south to Ratramnus of Corbie, asking whether the dog-headed men a missionary might meet in the north had reason and could be baptized. Nothing shows that Adam ever saw the reply.
sources: Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin, 'Adam Bremensis' and 'Rimbertus'
Ian N. Wood, 'Categorising the cynocephali' (austriaca.at/0xc1aa5572_0x002348d6.pdf), pp. 131-132
rimbert.journey.json; ratramnus_of_corbie.journey.json
suggested_refs: Rimbert's Vita Anskarii and the anonymous Vita Rimberti, Adam's sources for Gesta Book I
Ratramnus of Corbie, Epistola de cynocephalis

stops.name: Bremen, an archive that had forged its own foundation
stops.date_confidence: attested as method, reconstruction as to Adam's state of mind. That he worked from annals, saints' lives, letters, privileges and institutional books is standard and undisputed. Eric Knibbs, Ansgar, Rimbert and the Forged Foundations of Hamburg-Bremen (2011), argues from diplomatic and philological evidence that parts of the see's ninth-century foundation dossier were forged or interpolated. That Adam did not know this is inference, not testimony.
stops.campa: Beside the saints' lives lie the privileges: papal letters and imperial grants establishing Hamburg-Bremen's authority over the churches of the north, which the see produces whenever Cologne or the Danish kings dispute it. Adam copies them in good faith. Nine centuries on, Eric Knibbs will show from their diplomatic that a portion of that founding dossier was fabricated or interpolated in the ninth century itself. The canon defending his church's rights is arguing from documents made to be argued from.
sources: Eric Knibbs, Ansgar, Rimbert and the Forged Foundations of Hamburg-Bremen (Routledge, 2011), publisher description
Neue Deutsche Biographie, 'Adam von Bremen'
suggested_refs: The Hamburg-Bremen foundation privileges, re-examined by Knibbs in 2011

stops.name: Roskilde, seeking out the king of the Danes
stops.date_confidence: the journey is attested, the place is inference. Tschan: 'Very soon after he came to Bremen, therefore, he sought out Svein Estrithson, king of the Danes, to get first-hand information about the missions.' The NDB dates it probably 1067/68. Adam names Roskilde as the seat of Danish royalty at Gesta IV.5 but never says where the audience took place. The claim in circulation that Sven addressed Adam as 'son' does not appear anywhere in Tschan's text and is dropped.
stops.campa: Very soon after reaching Bremen he goes into Denmark to put questions to Sven Estridsen, who has reigned twenty years and whose people carried the missions Adam is trying to write down. The king talks; the canon writes. Sven becomes the single most cited living authority in the whole work, named at the head of report after report about islands, coasts, sun and ice. Adam calls his discourse veracious and very delightsome. Where in Denmark the audience happened, he never says.
sources: Tschan, translator's introduction to the Gesta
Adam of Bremen, Gesta III.liv and IV.5, tr. Tschan
Neue Deutsche Biographie, 'Adam von Bremen'
suggested_refs: Roskilde, named by Adam as the seat of Danish royalty, the standard identification for the audience

stops.name: Roskilde, the sun that does not set
stops.date_confidence: attested as text, inferred as scene. Gesta IV.38-40 records that the king of the Danes and many others attested the Icelandic midnight sun to Adam directly, and quotes Martianus Capella on the congealed sea beyond Thule. The dating and the placing of the conversation at Roskilde are ordering devices; Adam supplies neither.
stops.campa: The king tells him about Iceland: that at midsummer the sun stands over the land and does not go down, and that at midwinter the dark holds in the same way. This is how the whole fourth book will get made, a Roman author and a Danish mouth laid one against the other. Adam checks the report against Martianus Capella and Solinus, who wrote of a Thule beyond which the sea congeals after a day's sailing, and finds the old books and the living king in agreement. He notes that the king of the Danes and many others have attested the thing.
stops.quote: Beyond Thule, the sea is congealed after one day's navigation.
stops.quote_source: Martianus Capella, quoted by Adam of Bremen, Gesta IV.xxxix(38), tr. Francis J. Tschan
sources: Adam of Bremen, Gesta IV.38-40, tr. Tschan
suggested_refs: Martianus Capella, De nuptiis Philologiae et Mercurii, quoted inside Adam's own far-north chapter

stops.name: Roskilde, a people who come down from the highlands
stops.date_confidence: attested as text at Gesta IV.xxv(25), tr. Tschan, pp. 206-207, where Adam quotes the king directly with an interposed 'he said'. Tschan's note 83 identifies the people as Finns or Laplanders. An earlier reading of the passage gave 'three-year interval'; the text reads 'three-year period', and the sentence is two quoted spans, not one.
stops.campa: The king describes a people who come down out of the highlands onto the plains: small in stature, hardly matched by the Swedes for strength and agility, appearing without warning once in a year or once in three, and laying the whole region waste unless they are resisted with everything a man has. Adam sets it down as direct speech, with the king's voice inside his own sentence. Tschan, translating nine centuries later, will identify them as the Finns or the Laplanders.
stops.quote: 'Whence they come is not known. They come up unexpectedly,' he said, 'sometimes once in the course of a year or after a three-year period.'
stops.quote_source: Adam of Bremen, Gesta IV.xxv(25), tr. Francis J. Tschan, quoting Sven Estridsen
sources: Adam of Bremen, Gesta IV.xxv(25), tr. Tschan, and Tschan's note 83
suggested_refs: Tschan's note 83, identifying Sven's highland people with the Finns or Laplanders

stops.name: Roskilde, the north counted as one province
stops.date_confidence: attested as content, reconstruction as to motive. Adam records the see at Lund and the provostship at Dalby in Book IV. That Hamburg-Bremen's northern jurisdiction was contested, and that the Gesta functions as a defence of it, is the standard reading in Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin and the NDB. The framing of a single conversation at Roskilde as the moment of that purpose is this file's ordering, not a source's.
stops.campa: Every question he asks has a second purpose. Hamburg-Bremen claims to be the mother church of all the Danes, Swedes and Norwegians and the islands past them, and that claim is under pressure from Rome and from Danish kings who want bishops of their own. In his hands a catalogue of northern churches is also a title deed, geography written out as jurisdiction and filed where it can be produced. So he records the new establishments exactly, and to the letter: a see fixed at Lund, a provostship founded at Dalby.
sources: Adam of Bremen, Gesta IV, tr. Tschan, on Lund and Dalby
Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin, 'Adam Bremensis'
suggested_refs: The see of Lund and the provostship of Dalby, recorded by Adam as the northern church took its own shape

stops.name: Bremen, the archbishop watched
stops.date_confidence: attested as authorial practice; the date orders the segment. Book III of the Gesta is a topical character study of Adalbert rather than a chronicle, incorporating events of 1074 and 1075, so its composition postdates this pin. Adam is the only witness for much of it, and his authorial aside at III.lxxi(70) states the method in his own words.
stops.campa: Adalbert is the one man in the book Adam has actually seen: a Saxon of great family, brilliant, extravagant, ruined by his own reach at the imperial court, keeping seers and dwarfs about him at the end and refusing to sleep. Adam gives him a whole book, the third, and writes it as a portrait rather than a chronicle, virtues and vices arranged under headings. Then he asks the reader in advance to forgive him if the many-sided man escapes the method.
stops.quote: I beg you, reader, to forgive me if, in putting together under various topics the complex story of so many-sided a man, I have in this part directed every effort to writing truthfully, according to the canons of certainty and probability.
stops.quote_source: Adam of Bremen, Gesta III.lxxi(70), tr. Francis J. Tschan
sources: Adam of Bremen, Gesta III, tr. Tschan
Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin, 'Adam Bremensis'
suggested_refs: Gesta Book III, the character study of Archbishop Adalbert of Hamburg-Bremen

stops.name: Bremen, the body borne from Goslar
stops.date_confidence: the death is attested verbatim, the location of Adam is not. Gesta III.lxvii(66): 'Our most illustrious metropolitan Adalbert died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April in the tenth Indiction. That was the year of our Lord Jesus Christ one thousand and seventy-two.' III.lxviii(67) has the body borne from Goslar to Bremen. The claim repeated in some reference works that Adam attended the deathbed is supported by no passage placing him at Goslar, and is not carried here. The stop sits at Bremen because that is where Adam demonstrably was.
stops.campa: On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth indiction, the archbishop dies at the imperial palace of Goslar, a long road south of his cathedral, his estate come down to books, relics and vestments. The realm is thrown into what Adam calls great bewilderment. No line Adam ever wrote puts him at that bedside; he is somewhere at the other end of the road. The body travels north to Bremen over ground still hard with winter, and the chapter goes out along the road to meet it.
sources: Adam of Bremen, Gesta III.lxvii(66) and III.lxviii(67), tr. Tschan
Neue Deutsche Biographie, 'Adam von Bremen'
suggested_refs: The Kaiserpfalz at Goslar, where Adalbert died on 16 March 1072

stops.name: Bremen, the choir of the new basilica
stops.date_confidence: attested. Gesta III.lxviii(67): 'at length on the tenth day, that is, the feast of the Annunciation of the Blessed Mary... it was placed in a sepulcher in the middle of the choir of the new basilica that he himself had built.'
stops.campa: On the tenth day, the feast of the Annunciation, Adalbert goes into a sepulchre in the middle of the choir of the basilica he built himself. The chapter that has just lost its patron stands round the grave. Everything Adam will write about the see, from Willehad's first mission down to this morning, is written in the space that opens when the stone goes back down. He has been in this church six years, long enough to be a canon of it and not long enough to be from it.
sources: Adam of Bremen, Gesta III.lxviii(67), tr. Tschan
suggested_refs: The choir of the eleventh-century basilica at Bremen, Adalbert's burial place

stops.name: Bremen, the Gesta begun
stops.date_confidence: attested as sequence, approximate as date. The NDB states that Adam began the Hamburgische Kirchengeschichte after Adalbert's death. The month is an ordering device. The prologue is addressed to Archbishop Liemar, Adalbert's successor.
stops.campa: With the archbishop buried he begins in earnest: four books, running from the eighth-century mission to Willehad's Saxons down to a description of the islands of the north. He knows the shape of the objection before anyone makes it, and answers it in the prologue: that what he has written will be called fictitious and false, like Scipio's dream as Tully invented it. He writes it anyway, and addresses the whole thing to Liemar, the successor who has just arrived and knows nothing yet of the see he has been given.
stops.quote: I know that, as regularly happens with really novel works, I shall not lack critics. They will say that what I have written is fictitious and false, like Scipio's dreams as invented by Tully.
stops.quote_source: Adam of Bremen, Gesta, prologue, tr. Francis J. Tschan
sources: Adam of Bremen, Gesta, prologue, tr. Tschan
Neue Deutsche Biographie, 'Adam von Bremen'
suggested_refs: Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum, in four books, begun at Bremen after March 1072

stops.name: Bremen, Sven ever to be remembered
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from Schmeidler's compositional analysis, relayed by Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin, and a contradiction left standing. Within Book II Sven Estridsen is first described as living and reigning and later as 'ever to be remembered', which is taken to date the writing to the moment the news of his death arrived. That death is traditionally dated 28 April 1074; some modern chronologies give 1076, and the compositional inference moves with it.
stops.campa: Somewhere inside the second book the tense changes. Sven Estridsen is a king who lives and reigns; a few chapters on he is the king ever to be remembered. News of a death has reached Bremen with the work open on the desk, and the seam is still visible in the finished text. It fixes the writing of Book II to the summer or autumn of 1074, if the traditional date of the king's death holds. Some chronologies now put that death in 1076, and the seam moves with it.
sources: Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin, 'Adam Bremensis', citing Schmeidler's compositional analysis
suggested_refs: Schmeidler's reconstruction of the compositional stages of Gesta Book II

stops.name: Bremen, the archbishop under sentence
stops.date_confidence: attested as external history, reconstruction as to its bearing on the text. Liemar, archbishop 1072-1101 and the Gesta's dedicatee, supported Henry IV, was excommunicated by Gregory VII in 1075, and was absolved at Canossa in 1077. Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin treats this as the political backdrop of Adam's continued revision. Adam himself never mentions the quarrel, and he is not recorded anywhere near Canossa.
stops.campa: Liemar, Adalbert's successor and the man to whom the book is addressed, holds with Henry IV against Gregory VII and is excommunicated for it. Nothing in the four books says any of this out loud, and a reader who does not already know the quarrel will not learn it here. So the Gesta is being finished for a metropolitan under papal sentence, defending a northern jurisdiction that Rome is in these same years quietly taking apart, and every Danish and Swedish bishopric Adam catalogues is a stone in that defence. Two years on, Liemar is absolved at Canossa.
sources: Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin, 'Adam Bremensis'
Neue Deutsche Biographie, 'Adam von Bremen'
suggested_refs: Liemar of Bremen in the Investiture Contest, excommunicated 1075, absolved at Canossa 1077

stops.name: Bremen, the epilogue in verse
stops.date_confidence: attested as content, disputed as event. Book III carries events of 1074 and 1075, and the verse epilogue refers to Liemar's mediation in the Saxon conflict of 1075. The NDB dates the presentation of a dedication copy to 1075/76. Whether a physical presentation manuscript was actually delivered, or whether Adam kept and went on revising his own copy, divides Kristensen and Reuter from the older Schmeidler model and is not settled.
stops.campa: The third book carries events into 1074 and 1075, and the epilogue, written in verse, praises Liemar for his mediation in the Saxon revolt. Adam addresses his archbishop directly in meter and hands the work over. Whether a fair presentation copy physically changed hands in 1075 or 1076, or whether he kept his own manuscript on the desk and simply went on cutting into it for another five years, is a question modern editors answer in two incompatible ways. Kristensen and Reuter take one side of it. Schmeidler's older model takes the other, and the manuscripts do not decide between them.
sources: Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin, 'Adam Bremensis'
Neue Deutsche Biographie, 'Adam von Bremen'
suggested_refs: The verse epilogue of the Gesta, addressed to Archbishop Liemar

stops.name: Bremen, the additions that do not stop
stops.date_confidence: attested as a process, approximate as a date. The NDB: from 1075/76 Adam worked with various helpers on further additions and supplements, until about 1081. Schmeidler's MGH edition of 1917 reconstructs three lost authorial states, A, a and X, behind the surviving manuscript families. The 1078 pin is an ordering device inside that span.
stops.campa: The work is finished and he keeps working. Corrections go in, chapters swell, and scholia accumulate in the margins, some his and some in hands he never names, until the manuscript is a text with a commentary growing on it. This continues until about 1081. Schmeidler, reconstructing the transmission eight hundred years later, will need three separate lost authorial states, A, a and X, to explain what the surviving families of manuscripts inherited.
sources: Neue Deutsche Biographie, 'Adam von Bremen'
Bernhard Schmeidler, MGH SS rer. Germ. 2 (dmgh.de/mgh_ss_rer_germ_2)
suggested_refs: Schmeidler's three reconstructed authorial states of the Gesta: A, a, X

stops.name: Bremen, a world mapped by ear
stops.date_confidence: attested as the character of Book IV, reconstruction as to the mechanics. That the Descriptio insularum aquilonis is descriptive geography rather than episcopal history is plain from the text; that Adam's information came from Sven Estridsen, from Adalbert, from named individual informants, and from Solinus and Martianus Capella is stated in the text itself. No source shows Adam travelling beyond Denmark. The 1080 pin orders the segment that follows.
stops.campa: The fourth book is a different animal from the three before it: not a history of bishops but a description of the islands of the north, coast by coast and people by people, out to the place where the record gives way. He is mapping a world by ear. He has been no further than Denmark, and everything past that comes from the king's talk, from sailors and merchants putting in at the Weser, from Adalbert's own recollections, and from Solinus and Martianus Capella on the shelf above the desk.
sources: Adam of Bremen, Gesta IV (Descriptio insularum aquilonis), tr. Tschan
Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin, 'Adam Bremensis'
suggested_refs: Descriptio insularum aquilonis, the fourth book of the Gesta

segments.name: The Baltic Shore, Taken on Report

stops.name: Helgoland, the pirates' tithe
stops.date_confidence: attested as Adam's text, Gesta IV.3, tr. Tschan. Adam never travelled to Helgoland, and no source places him on any island. This stop and those following map the north as his fourth book describes it, not a route he walked. His alternative name for the island, Fositesland, comes from the Vita Willibrordi. The date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: A small island off the Frisian coast, cliff-walled, holy to sailors and holiest of all to pirates. Adam reports that men who plunder there come to grief afterwards, and that they have learned to give the hermits living on the rock a tithe of their booty, out of fear of shipwreck rather than fear of God. The cattle grazing on it are not to be touched, and the spring is drunk from in silence. He calls the island Fositesland, after the old life of Willibrord, and then gives the name the sea gives it: Hezgland, the holy land.
sources: Adam of Bremen, Gesta IV.3, tr. Tschan
suggested_refs: The Vita Willibrordi, source of Adam's name Fositesland for Helgoland

stops.name: Schleswig, the port for Jumne
stops.date_confidence: attested as Adam's text, Gesta II.19, tr. Tschan: 'for by the sea route one boards ship at Schleswig or Oldenburg to get to Jumne.' Adam is not recorded at Schleswig; the pin 54.5236, 9.5533 is the canonical Schleswig coordinate already used in the Rimbert file.
stops.campa: The Baltic in his book is not a blank space with monsters drawn in the corners. It is a set of crossings with sailing times attached to each one, the monsters kept further out where the crossings stop, and the counting begins at this harbour. At Schleswig on the Schlei, or else at Oldenburg, a man bound for the Slavic emporium at the mouth of the Oder boards his ship. Adam gives directions like someone who has asked the right men at a quay: which harbour, which heading, how many days out, what a ship carries when it goes.
sources: Adam of Bremen, Gesta II.19, tr. Tschan
rimbert.journey.json, for the canonical Schleswig pin
suggested_refs: The Schlei and the harbour of Schleswig, Adam's named point of departure for the Baltic

stops.name: Jumne, the largest city in Europe
stops.date_confidence: attested as Adam's text, Gesta II.19, tr. Tschan; the superlative is his, not this file's. Adam never went there. The identification of Jumne with Wolin at the Oder mouth is the standard modern one. Excavation at Wolin has confirmed a substantial early medieval emporium; nothing confirms the scale Adam claims.
stops.campa: At the Oder's mouth stands a town Adam calls Jumne, truly the largest of all the cities of Europe, where Slavs and Greeks and Saxons trade, where Christianity may be believed but not practised in the open, and where a fire burns that the inhabitants call Greek fire and he calls the pot of Vulcan. Every good of the north passes through it, and Adam gives it walls, a harbour and a population without ever having stood in front of any of them. Archaeology at Wolin has found a large early medieval emporium. It has not found the largest city in Europe.
sources: Adam of Bremen, Gesta II.19, tr. Tschan
suggested_refs: The early medieval emporium at Wolin, standard identification of Adam's Jumne

stops.name: Rethra, nine gates and a lake
stops.date_confidence: attested as Adam's text, Gesta II.18, tr. Tschan; the coordinate is a guess. Tschan's own note places the temple on an island in the Tollensee near modern Feldberg, but the site has never been conclusively excavated or located, and the pin here follows the direction Adam points rather than any confirmed find. Adam did not go there.
stops.campa: Among the Slavic Retharii, Adam sets a temple city: nine gates, a deep lake all round it, a wooden bridge that only sacrificers and men seeking oracles may cross, and inside, a golden idol of the god Redigast. The description reaches him at second or third hand, from men who traded with the Slavs or fought them. It is built exactly like the Uppsala temple he will describe two books later: gold, a sacred enclosure, a fixed count of gates. Tschan's note puts the place on an island in the Tollensee, somewhere in the direction Adam is pointing. No excavation has ever found it.
sources: Adam of Bremen, Gesta II.18, tr. Tschan, with Tschan's note on the Tollensee

stops.name: Samland, the humane people of the amber coast
stops.date_confidence: attested as Adam's text, Gesta IV.18, tr. Tschan. Adam never travelled the eastern Baltic. The martyrdom of Adalbert of Prague among the Prussians in 997 is independently attested and is Adam's own cross-reference, not this file's addition.
stops.campa: Far east along the Baltic he finds the Sembi, or Prussians, and gives them the best character in the book: a most humane people, who put out to sea to help men in danger from storms or from pirates. They hold gold and silver cheap. They have marten furs so fine that the whole north is sick with wanting them, and they will trade one of them for a woollen cloak without thinking they have been cheated. They are also, he notes without altering his tone, the people at whose hands Adalbert, the illustrious bishop of the Bohemians, was crowned with martyrdom.
sources: Adam of Bremen, Gesta IV.18, tr. Tschan

stops.name: Ostrogard, the men who bark
stops.date_confidence: attested as a statement Adam makes, at Gesta IV.19, tr. Tschan; not as fact. Adam never went to Rus'. Ostrogard is glossed by Adam's own scholiast as Russia broadly and by Tschan's apparatus alternatively as Novgorod or Ostrov; the Novgorod pin follows the conventional identification and the ambiguity is real.
stops.campa: The report he is given is that the dog-headed men are not a rumour but a commodity: taken somewhere further off, brought west, and shown in Russia as captives. Adam writes it in the flat voice he uses for a market price. Two centuries earlier an archbishop of this same see had thought the question serious enough to send a letter into Frankish country asking whether such a creature had reason and could be baptized. Adam asks nothing. He records that they bark.
stops.quote: The Cynocephali are men who have their heads on their breasts. They are often seen in Russia as captives and they voice their words in barks.
stops.quote_source: Adam of Bremen, Gesta IV.xix(19), tr. Francis J. Tschan

stops.name: Kiev, rival of the sceptre of Constantinople
stops.date_confidence: attested as Adam's text at Gesta II.xxii(19), tr. Tschan; Adam never went to Russia. A conflation in circulation should be flagged: the fourteen days' sail from Jumne is to Ostrogard, and Kiev is named in the following sentence as the largest city of Russia. Adam does not say that Kiev is fourteen days from Jumne.
stops.campa: Fourteen days' sail up from Jumne brings a ship to Ostrogard of Russia. Then, in the next breath, the largest city of Russia: Kiev, which Adam calls a rival of the sceptre of Constantinople and the brightest ornament of Greece. He is writing for a German cathedral chapter that has never seen either city and never will, and he puts Kiev beside Constantinople as though the comparison needed no defending. He has not been there. He can nonetheless tell a reader how many days out it lies, in which direction, and what he will find on arrival.
sources: Adam of Bremen, Gesta II.xxii(19), tr. Tschan

stops.name: The Baltic shore, the land of women
stops.date_confidence: attested as Adam's text at Gesta IV.19, tr. Tschan, and as tradition only in substance. Adam does not locate the land of women more precisely than 'round about the shore of the Baltic Sea'; the coordinate is a representative point on the Courland coast and pins a report, not a place. Ian Wood's study of the passage is the standard modern discussion.
stops.campa: Round about the shore of the sea, it is said, live the Amazons, in what is now called the land of women. Adam weighs how they conceive: by merchants passing through, or by the captives they hold, or by the monsters that are not rare in those parts. A rival account has them made pregnant by a mouthful of water, and this explanation he finds the more credible. The daughters grow into beautiful women and drive men off. The sons come out with the heads of dogs.
stops.quote: And when these women come to give birth, if the offspring be of the male sex, they become Cynocephali; if of the feminine kind, they become most beautiful women.

stops.name: Birka, the port of Saint Ansgar
stops.date_confidence: attested as Adam's text at Gesta IV.20 and scholion 127, tr. Tschan; Adam never went to Sweden. The pin 59.3325, 17.5407 is the canonical Birka coordinate already used in the Rimbert file. That the Björkö emporium had in fact been abandoned since the later tenth century is modern archaeology, not Adam's information, and is marked as such.
stops.campa: In central Sweden, lying opposite Jumne across the water, Adam places Björkö, which his metropolitan appointed as a see for the peoples of the eastern shore. He sets it down as a working metropolis. By the time that sentence is written the town has lain abandoned for a hundred years, and nobody in Bremen has any way of knowing it. What he does know he uses: he claims the place for Hamburg-Bremen by naming its dead, the port Ansgar sailed to, the burial mound of Archbishop Unni, the island he calls a hospice for the confessors of his own church.

stops.name: Uppsala, the temple decked out in gold
stops.date_confidence: attested as Adam's text at Gesta IV.xxvi(26) and scholion 139(135), tr. Tschan; explicitly hearsay in his own framing, and he never went to Sweden. Anders Hultgard's work treats the account as unreliable in specific detail without dismissing it outright. Note one correction to a claim in circulation: the golden chain hangs from the gables, it does not girdle the building.
stops.campa: Not far from Sigtuna and Björkö, he says, the Swedes keep a temple of gold. Thor is enthroned in the middle of it because he governs the air, thunder, wind, rain and crops; Wotan, which is to say fury, sits on one side and makes war; Frikko sits on the other and gives peace and pleasure to mortals. A golden chain hangs down over the gable and throws its glitter at anyone approaching, because the shrine stands on level ground with hills all round it like a theatre.
stops.quote: In this temple, entirely decked out in gold, the people worship the statues of three gods in such wise that the mightiest of them, Thor, occupies a throne in the middle of the chamber; Wotan and Frikko have places on either side.
stops.quote_source: Adam of Bremen, Gesta IV.xxvi(26), tr. Francis J. Tschan

stops.name: Uppsala, nine heads of every living thing
stops.date_confidence: attested as Adam's text at Gesta IV.xxvii(27), tr. Tschan, and as his own claim of an informant; not as fact, and not as anything he saw. Excavation at Gamla Uppsala has established a major elite and ritual site: Lindqvist's postholes of 1926, reread by Alkarp and Price in 2005 as several building phases, and a mid-fifth-century double row of 144 posts found in 2013, six centuries too early to be Adam's temple.
stops.campa: Every nine years, he reports, there is a festival at Uppsala that no man in any Swedish province may absent himself from, and the sacrifice is of this nature: of every living thing that is male, nine heads, with whose blood it is customary to placate gods of that sort. The bodies hang in the grove beside the temple, dogs and horses among the men. Gamla Uppsala has yielded a hall, postholes and a royal cult site, and no building that answers his. For this chapter, unusually, he names his informant and gives the man's age.
stops.quote: A Christian seventy-two years old told me that he had seen their bodies suspended promiscuously.
stops.quote_source: Adam of Bremen, Gesta IV.xxvii(27), tr. Francis J. Tschan

stops.name: Hälsingland, the Rhiphaean mountains
stops.date_confidence: attested as Adam's text at Gesta IV.xxv(25) and scholion 157(132-133), tr. Tschan; the Rhiphaean range is a classical topos with no fixed real referent. The pin follows Adam's own gloss, which places Hälsingland, the land of the Skritefingi, in the midst of the mountains called Rhiphaean. A coordinate on the Kola peninsula, sometimes proposed, extrapolates north-eastward in a direction Adam's own scholium does not support.
stops.campa: Past the settled provinces the map turns into a list. The mountains Roman writers call the Rhiphaean range are terrible for their perpetual snows, and without that frost the Skritefingi living among them cannot survive; they outrun wild beasts on foot. Then, in order: the Amazons, the dog-heads, the one-eyed, the one-footed hoppers Solinus named, and the eaters of human flesh. Adam shuns them and passes them over in silence, having first written every one of them down.
stops.quote: There are Amazons, and Cynocephali, and Cyclops who have one eye on their foreheads; there are those Solinus calls Himantopodes, who hop on one foot, and those who delight in human flesh as food, and as they are shunned, so may they also rightfully be passed over in silence.
stops.quote_source: Adam of Bremen, Gesta IV.xxv(25), tr. Francis J. Tschan

stops.name: Trondheim, the body of Olaf
stops.date_confidence: attested as Adam's text at Gesta IV.32-33, tr. Tschan; Adam never went to Norway. The pin 63.4305, 10.3951 is the canonical Nidaros coordinate already used in the Leif Erikson file. Olaf Haraldsson fell at Stiklestad in 1030, which is external history and not drawn from Adam.
stops.campa: The metropolitan city of the Norwegians, he writes, is now graced with churches and thronged by great crowds of people. Olaf Haraldsson fell at Stiklestad in 1030, and forty-five years later a canon in Bremen is writing the pilgrimage up as settled northern geography. In the city lies the body of the most blessed Olaf, king and martyr, and at that tomb the Lord works such miraculous cures to this day that men come from far-off countries hoping to be helped by his merits.

stops.name: Helgeland, fourteen days of sun
stops.date_confidence: attested as Adam's text at Gesta IV.37, tr. Tschan, and corrected inside his own manuscript. Adam calls Helgeland the third of the far northern islands; a scholiast notes in the margin that it is a mainland district, not an island. The coordinate is a representative point on the Helgeland coast. Adam did not go there.
stops.campa: The third of the far northern islands, nearer to Norway than the others and no smaller than they are. Adam says the sun stands over the land there for fourteen days together at the solstice and withdraws for as many in the winter. The book comes down with the text and the second thoughts on the same page: his own scholiast, writing in the margin, notes that Helgeland is not an island at all but a district of the mainland. Neither statement is struck out.

stops.name: Iceland, where the Frisians made land
stops.date_confidence: attested as Adam's text at Gesta IV.xl(39)-IV.40, tr. Tschan, and reported to him by Adalbert. The voyage is dated by Adam to the days of Adalbert's predecessor, not to Adalbert's own pontificate: 'Archbishop Adalbert of blessed memory likewise told us that in the days of his predecessor certain noble men of Frisia spread sail to the north.' The pin 64.9631, -19.0208 is the canonical Iceland coordinate already used in the Leif Erikson file. Adam never sailed.
stops.campa: Adalbert had told him a story from his predecessor's day: certain noble men of Frisia who spread sail north from the mouth of the Weser to test the claim that nothing lay that way except open sea. They left Denmark on one hand and Britain on the other, passed the Orkneys keeping them to port, and came ashore after a long passage on icy Iceland. The island, Adam writes elsewhere, where nobody lies and nobody steals, whose bishop is king, whose people keep their cattle in caves.

stops.name: Vinland, an island the king names
stops.date_confidence: attested as Adam's text at Gesta IV.xxxix(38), tr. Tschan, and as the earliest surviving written European notice of Vinland. Adam gives no coordinates and no sailing directions; the pin is a placeholder in the western ocean for the report itself. He did not go, names no captain and no year, and attributes the whole of it to the Danes. L'Anse aux Meadows, excavated by the Ingstads from 1961 after Helge Ingstad located it in 1960, is the only confirmed Norse site in North America and is a modern hypothesis about the sagas, not about Adam.
stops.campa: Beyond the ice, the king of the Danes tells him of one more island in that ocean which many have found: called Vinland, because vines grow there wild and give excellent wine, and because grain nobody sowed comes up there in abundance. Adam insists on the standing of the report. He has it not from fabulous tales but from the trustworthy relation of the Danes. He names no captain and no year. The voyages behind the king's story are the ones the Icelandic sagas will later put in the hands of Leif Eriksson.
stops.quote: It is called Vinland because vines producing excellent wine grow wild there.
stops.quote_source: Adam of Bremen, Gesta IV.xxxix(38), tr. Francis J. Tschan

stops.name: The frozen sea, the edge of the record
stops.date_confidence: attested as Adam's text at Gesta IV.40, tr. Tschan; the place is not a place. Adam gives no coordinates for the numbing ocean and its whirling current, which is a classical topos of the world's edge. The pin is symbolic, set in the North Atlantic beyond Iceland along the line the Frisian story runs, and it maps a passage of writing rather than a location.
stops.campa: Pressing north from Iceland the Frisians go into that numbing ocean's dark mist, which no eye can penetrate, and the current of the fluctuating ocean whirls back toward its own hidden fountainhead and drags the ships after it with furious force. Adam's geography ends here, not at a coast but at an abyss, and everything he has gathered from kings, sailors and Roman books runs out together at the one line. The men call on God's mercy. Some are swallowed.
sources: Adam of Bremen, Gesta IV.40, tr. Tschan

stops.name: Bremen, the last correction
stops.date_confidence: attested as a negative fact. The NDB gives about 1081 as the end of Adam's own additions and 1085 as the latest possible year of his death; Tschan writes that after 1085 there is no trace of Adam's hand in the text or scholia. The range sometimes given as 1085-90 is not supported by any source checked here; every source stops at 1085.
stops.campa: After about 1081 nothing in the manuscript any longer looks like the author. Scholia keep accumulating, but in other men's hands, and the editorial work runs on into the middle eighties without him. There is no illness recorded, no deathbed scene, no successor named, no last words, no will. A book that spends four hundred pages establishing when each archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen died, and in which indiction, and by whose reckoning, does not record the death of the man who wrote it.
sources: Neue Deutsche Biographie, 'Adam von Bremen'

stops.name: Bremen, magister Adam, the twelfth of October
stops.date_confidence: the day is attested, the year is not, and the place is inference. Tschan: 'In the Dyptichon Bremense a magister Adam is noted as having died on October 12, but, as was the rule in such records, without mention of the year.' Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin gives 12 October in an unknown year between 1081 and 1085. The file dates the stop 1085-10-12 only to place it last in sequence. No source states a place of death or a burial site; Bremen is inferred from residence, and the grave is a documented gap.
stops.campa: The cathedral necrology carries one line: magister Adam, the twelfth of October. No year, as the custom of such books is. The day is fixed forever and the year is gone. Where he was buried nobody wrote down. The German reference works on Bremen cathedral list every tomb and plaque in the building, and cite him again and again as their source for its construction under Adalbrand and Adalbert. They never once list him among the men lying inside it. No monument, no bust, no plaque, no stone.

stops.name: Leiden, the oldest surviving leaves
stops.date_confidence: attested. Leiden, Universiteitsbibliotheek, Voss. Lat. Q. 123 (siglum A2), copied around 1100, containing excerpts from Gesta II.16-22 and Book IV on leaves later cut down by a binder, is the oldest surviving witness; the Leiden catalogue record carries the description. That Book IV began circulating separately from about 1100 is reported by Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin. Adam's own manuscript does not survive in any form.
stops.campa: Adam's own manuscript is gone, and so is every copy made while he was alive. What survives first is a set of excerpts, Book II chapters sixteen to twenty-two and pieces of Book IV, written out around 1100 and later trimmed by a binder who needed the leaves to fit something else. Around the same time the fourth book starts to travel on its own, detached from the three books of archbishops it was written to serve. The description of the north outlives the history it was fastened to.

stops.name: Copenhagen, the first printing
stops.date_confidence: attested, and it corrects a claim in wide circulation. Tschan's introduction is explicit: 'Of the printings already noted, those of B2 by Vedel in 1579 and of C2 by Lindenbrog in 1595, only the latter was republished.' Danish sources confirm Vedel issued the first printed edition of Adam's church history in 1579, at Copenhagen. German Wikipedia's article on the Gesta names Lindenbrog's 1595 Leiden printing as the first edition; that contradiction is flagged and resolved in Tschan's favour, and the resolution is stated rather than assumed.
stops.campa: Five hundred years after it was written, the Danish historiographer Anders Sørensen Vedel puts the Gesta into print at Copenhagen, working from a text of the B family whose ancestor had been copied at Sorø in 1161 or 1162. Sixteen years later Erpold Lindenbrog prints a different recension at Leiden, from a codex lent him by Heinrich Rantzau and since lost. It is Lindenbrog's edition that gets reprinted and remembered, and reference works still hand him a priority that belongs to Vedel.
sources: Tschan, translator's introduction to the Gesta

stops.name: Copenhagen, codex z burns
stops.date_confidence: attested as a loss, approximate as a day. Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin records that codex z, a B-family manuscript of 1161/62, was destroyed in the Copenhagen fire of 1728 and survives only partially through later copies. The fire ran from 20 to 23 October 1728; the stop takes its first day.
stops.campa: The B-family manuscript written at Sorø in 1161 or 1162, the oldest complete witness anybody had, is in Copenhagen when the city burns, and it goes with everything else. What is left of it is whatever earlier copyists happened to have transcribed before the fire, and they were not trying to save anything, only to have a reading copy of their own. So Adam's text now stands in places as a reconstruction of a lost copy of a lost original, held up by the incidental labour of men who found it worth writing out.
sources: Medieval Nordic Literature in Latin, 'Adam Bremensis'

stops.name: Hannover, the three lost states
stops.date_confidence: attested. Johann Martin Lappenberg edited the Gesta for MGH Scriptores VII in 1846, working from A1; Bernhard Schmeidler's edition of 1917 in the MGH Scriptores rerum Germanicarum in usum scholarum remains the scholarly standard and reconstructs three lost authorial states, A, a and X. Tschan's English translation appeared from Columbia University Press in 1959. The Vienna manuscript ÖNB Cod. 521 (A1), long dated to around 1200, is dated by German Wikipedia to the first half of the thirteenth century.
stops.campa: Johann Martin Lappenberg edits the Gesta for the Monumenta Germaniae Historica in 1846, working from the Vienna manuscript. Seventy years later Bernhard Schmeidler produces the edition still in use, and to make the surviving families of manuscripts agree he has to posit three authorial states that no longer exist: A, a and X, three successive conditions of a book being revised by a man who never stopped revising it. In 1959 Francis Tschan puts the whole thing into English.
